His third, as far as Rom. xix-xxviii THE ACTS
But ye shall receive power — and shall be witnesses to me - That is, ye shall be empowered to witness my Gospel, both by your preaching and suffering.

glossa.text: *I made a discourse.* That is, I wrote: because to write is to work. Or he says it thus, because by his deeds he deserved to be the writer of the Gospel. *I made.* The whole book of the Gospel is called one discourse, in that it has one sense: or the singular stands for the plural. The Gospel is a good announcement, by which is announced rest after labour, a kingdom after servitude, life after death. *Of all things.* Of the sayings and deeds of Christ which he judged worthy of his office or fit for his dispensation. *O Theophilus.* Theophilus is the same as friend of God, or lover of God: and if thou art a friend of God, it is written for thee. *Which Jesus began to do.* From the baptism of John by which Jesus was baptized, *until the day* on which he was taken up into heaven: because Luke wove the discourses concerning that whole time, who at the end of the Gospel wrote thus: *When he had blessed, he departed from them and was carried into heaven. To do.* He appoints or instructs a good teacher, one who does what he teaches.

*Giving commandment to the apostles* to preach the Gospel *through the Holy Spirit,* through whom the Gospel was preached, because he inspired the words and bestowed confidence. Or, *giving commandment through the Holy Spirit,* that is, what the Son commands, this the Holy Spirit also commands. Or, he gave the commandment on account of the Spirit, because he would not command unless the Spirit were about to come. *He chose.* This turns to the praise of the apostles, whose acts he purposes to write. *Taken up.* Taken up by the Divinity, or by a cloud, as true man.

*Alive.* A living and proper body, not a phantasmal one, which the apostles also recognized as most well known. Or alive, in that after death he was living. Or alive, that is, no more to die. *Through days.* Yet he did not appear to them through forty continuous days: for John says that after the day of the resurrection four other days intervened. After which he appeared again through forty: because he had been dead for forty hours, for forty days he confirms that he lives. And by the forty a type of the present age may be understood, in which Christ is engaged in the Church: or because man, consisting of four elements, is instructed against the transgression of the Decalogue.

*Eating together with them.* He announces the signs of a true body, because not by one sense of the body, but by sight, by hearing, by touch, by appearing, by speaking, by eating together, he proved that he had risen. *The promise,* which he promised through Joel, as is had in what follows: and if it was made by Christ, yet it will be fulfilled by the Father. Or it is called *of the Father,* because it is promised in his Word, that is, in Christ.

*For John. ((BEDA.))* When the Lord said: For John baptized with water, but you, etc., *as far as* that which was not done in the baptism of John.

Baptism is given in two natures, namely the bodily and the spiritual: because the man who is baptized consists of two: namely of body and of soul, yet baptism is one, as the man is one.

*But you,* etc. When Peter denied, the apostles were not baptized; not with water, but with the spirit: for after the resurrection it was said: *But you shall be baptized with the Holy Spirit.* For they had not yet been confirmed by the resurrection of Christ and by the mission of the Spirit. But as circumcision was not necessary to the just before it was commanded to Abraham and to his posterity: so after the sacrament of the New Testament, that is baptism, was given in the place of circumcision by the Lord saying: *Unless a man be born again of water and the Holy Spirit ((Joan. III))*, etc., it is certain that none belongs to the body of Christ save the baptized, apart from those to whom the passion is reckoned in place of baptism. Likewise it is written when Paul was baptized: and it is not written when the other apostles were baptized: but we ought to understand that they were baptized on account of that: *Unless a man be born again,* etc.

*It is not for you to know.* He does not say, it will not be, but *it is not:* noting that they are still weak, and therefore not fit for the knowing of the secret: but when he says: *It is not for you to know,* he shows that he himself knows, whose are all things that are the Father's, but that it is not expedient for them to know, but that they should so live as though they were to be judged daily. *Which the Father.* The time of that kingdom, he says, is so secret that it lies open only to the knowledge of the Father, *but you shall receive the power of the Holy Spirit,* that what through the weakness of the flesh you cannot do, you may be able to do out of the power of the Holy Spirit. *In his own power.* This he said excusably as true man, but there is only one power of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit: the Son also is the power of the Father.

*But you shall receive.* The knowledge of the times is taken away, but the divine help of which they stand in need is applied: in this manner, when something is taken from children, another thing is given lest they be utterly saddened. *Of the Holy Spirit coming upon you.* When the Spirit shall come upon you, he will not bring the kingdom of Israel, or the kingdom of God in Israel, as you think, but he will bestow upon you the power of bearing witness of me, and the time of that kingdom is so far off, that first the fame of the Gospel shall run through not only Jerusalem, but all the borders of Judaea and of Samaria, and even the bounds of the world round about. *In Jerusalem and in all Judaea.* The consequence of order is preserved in the names of the places: to Jerusalem succeeds the nearest province of Judaea, to which Samaria is joined by situation, and thereafter the fellowship of the whole earth is brought in. *In Jerusalem.* Mystically: in the vision of peace, in the confession of the true faith: in the keeping of the commandments of God: and he foretold that they would preach among those who shall have made themselves strangers from the earth, through whom, as through the spokes of a wheel, from the middle of the earth where he wrought salvation, spiritual grace and saving doctrine flowed out through the whole world.

*And when he had said these things.* Mark records it otherwise, saying: *And the Lord Jesus indeed, after he had spoken to them, was taken up into heaven ((Matth. XXVIII))*. But because Luke added more significantly: *When he had said these things, he was lifted up,* he shows that, those discourses being finished which he had recorded, the Lord ascended the heavens.

*Galilaeans, why stand you looking up to heaven?* In whom there ought to be a more prudent understanding, because the Galilaeans excelled the rest of the Jews in wisdom. Or, Galilaeans, the changeable, because by the instability of their sense they will have forgotten the commandments of God.

notes.text: Subdue — He speaks this in the name of the whole church, to which all particular believers were to submit themselves in the Lord.

Chuse — He will appoint and bestow upon us. Inheritance - The presence and worship, and blessing of God. This God had chosen for the Israelites and resolved to chuse or set apart for the Gentiles. Of Jacob - Of the people of Jacob or Israel, who are frequently called Jacob, for these did actually enjoy the presence of God in his sanctuary. Loved - Not for any peculiar worth in them, but for his free love to them, as he declareth, Deut. vii, 7, 8.

God — This is meant literally of the ark: but mystically of Christ's ascension into heaven, as may be gathered by comparing this with Eph. iv, 8, where the like words uttered concerning the ark upon the same occasion, chap. lxviii, 18, are directly applied to Christ's ascension.

The king — Not only ours, but of all the nations of the world. Sing - Not formally and carelessly, but seriously, considering the greatness of this king whom you praise, and what abundant cause you have to praise him.

The throne — Heaven is often called God's throne, whence God is said to behold and to rule all nations; of which general dominion of God, he here speaks. And Christ sits at his father's right-hand, for that purpose.

The princes — The Gentiles, who were divided in their principles, and interests, and religions, are now united and gathered together to Christ, laying their scepters at his feet, and jointly owning his worship and service. And altho' he mentions their conversion only, yet the conversion of their people might reasonably be supposed. Of the God - He doth not say the people of Abraham, lest this should be appropriated to the Israelites; but the people of the God of Abraham who worship the God of Abraham, whether they be Jews or Gentiles. The Shields - The princes or rulers, who are called shields, Hosea iv, 18, because by their office they are the common prosecutors of all their people. These are the Lord's, at his disposal, or subject to his dominion, both as to their hearts and kingdoms. Exalted - By this means God shall be greatly glorified. The glory and excellency of the church, ver. 1-3. Which God preserves from her enemies, ver. 4-8. God is praised for this, ver. 9, 10. Who effectually provides for its safety, ver. 11-14 A song and psalm for the sons of Korah.

glossa.text: *All ye Gentiles.* ((AUG.)) As if he should say: they insult, the boys, saying: *Bald head, bald head,* you, all the Gentiles to whom grace has passed over: *Clap your hands,* etc. The Gentiles to whom grace has passed over, and whom in the former psalm he called to faith, he invites to praise.
*High.* ((HIER.)) Powerful in what he wills. *Terrible.* ((REMIG.)) Because he is to judge in power.

*He hath subdued the peoples unto us.* ((CASS.)) This befits faithful men, to whom all outsiders are made subject, or, he has subjected to himself those who are to be associated with us. *The peoples,* the Jews. *Unto us. ((Ibid.))* Namely to the universal Church; this it befits all the faithful to say, to whom outsiders are made subject. *Under the feet. ((Ibid.))* By *feet,* understand preachers, to whom the peoples are made subject. ((AUG.)) *Under the feet.* So is the Church exalted, that it has those not yet believing under its feet.

*He hath chosen for us,* etc. Or in the person of the Apostles, he chose to give us his inheritance, of many peoples, that we may cultivate it, striking their hearts with the sword of preaching, and destroying their malice. *The inheritance.* ((AUG.)) The heavenly inheritance is the beauty of the Christian people, in which he shall be comely, shining as the sun, who now is abject. *The beauty of Jacob which,* etc. That is, those like to Jacob or signed by Jacob, who give earthly things for heavenly, as Jacob did, which was the grace of God, because *he loved him, Esau being reprobate.*

*He is ascended.* ((CASS.)) Diapsalma, the ascension and the kingdom of God is described, whence he urgently admonishes to sing psalms. *In jubilation.* ((AUG.)) The joy of the wondering Apostles, etc., *as far as* what can neither be kept silent nor be uttered.
*Sing ye psalms.* ((CASS.)) Praise by works: very salutary is that which is so often repeated, because it is God who creates, and a king governing the things created.

*Of all the earth. ((Ibid.))* Not as Jupiter of Crete, Mars of Thrace. *Wisely.* He teaches how one ought to sing psalms. Of old they sang psalms without understanding, while they worshipped stones. ((AUG.)) No one does wisely what he does not understand.
*He shall reign. ((Ibid.))* Now is this prophecy fulfilled: *God sitteth upon the holy seat. The holy seat.* ((AUG.)) Thrones, Virtues, and the saints.

*The princes of the peoples.* ((CASS.)) The first-fruits of all the Gentiles came together by believing in Christ, because, the Jews being cast out, the Gentiles succeed into the sons of Abraham, having the promise, because the Jews were lifted up in pride. ((HIER., CASS.)) Or *the strong gods,* namely the Apostles, whom neither death nor life shall separate from the charity of Christ. *Lifted up,* by miracles and doctrine.

notes.text: Since I heard of your faith and love — That is, of their perseverance and increase therein.
I cease not — In all my solemn addresses to God. To give thanks for you, making mention of you in my prayers - So he did of all the churches, Col. i, 9.

That the Father of that infinite glory which shines in the face of Christ, from whom also we receive the glorious inheritance, ver. 18, may give you the Spirit of wisdom and Revelation — The same who is the Spirit of promise is also, in the progress of the faithful, the Spirit of wisdom and Revelation; making them wise unto salvation, and revealing to them the deep things of God. He is here speaking of that wisdom and Revelation which are common to all real Christians.

The eyes of your understanding — It is with these alone that we discern the things of God. Being first opened, and then enlightened - By his Spirit. That ye may know what is the hope of his calling - That ye may experimentally and delightfully know what are the blessings which God has called you to hope for by his word and his Spirit. And what is the riches of the glory of his inheritance in the saints - What an immense treasure of blessedness he hath provided as an inheritance for holy souls.

And what the exceeding greatness of his power toward us who believe — Both in quickening our dead souls, and preserving them in spiritual life. According to the power which he exerted in Christ, raising him from the dead - By the very same almighty power whereby he raised Christ; for no less would suffice.

And he hath seated him at his own right hand — That is, he hath exalted him in his human nature, as a recompence for his sufferings, to a quiet, everlasting possession of all possible blessedness, majesty, and glory.

Far above all principality, and power, and might, and dominion — That is, God hath invested him with uncontrollable authority over all demons in hell, all angels in heaven, and all the princes and potentates on earth. And every name that is named - We know the king is above all, though we cannot name all the officers of his court. So we know that Christ is above all, though we are not able to name all his subjects. Not only in this world, but also in that which is to come - The world to come is so styled, not because it does not yet exist, but because it is not yet visible. Principalities and powers are named now; but those also who are not even named in this world, but shall be revealed in the world to come, are all subject to Christ.

And he hath given him to be head over all things to the church — An head both of guidance and government, and likewise of life and influence, to the whole and every member of it. All these stand in the nearest union with him, and have as continual and effectual a communication of activity, growth, and strength from him, as the natural body from its head.

The fulness of him that filleth all in all — It is hard to say in what sense this can be spoken of the church; but the sense is easy and natural, if we refer it to Christ, who is the fulness of the Father.

glossa.text: *Therefore.* The benefits conferred upon the human race, or upon the apostles, or upon the Ephesians having been enumerated, the Apostle subjoins what he thinks concerning their benefits, namely that he gives thanks, and asks that more be added, lest they be proud, but stretch beyond.
*That God,* etc. As if he should say: to obtain it I put forward not merits, but that he is God and the Father of Christ, etc.

*The eyes of the heart.* In his own image, therefore, know thou its author, who is not attained by bodily sense. Do not, therefore, think that God is attained by bodily sense, but with the eyes of the mind hear him. In the body, where the members are diverse, thou hearest in one place, thou seest in another. But in thy heart, where diverse members are not found, there thou hearest where thou seest. And to this end may he enlighten the eyes. *That you may know,* etc. This he says that they may be the more inclined: because when they shall fully know what the fruit of believers is, they will become the more inclined toward the cultivating of religion. Or thus: that hope be taken properly. And the sense is: That you may know what it is, namely his will *voluntas*; read *vocatio*, "calling", that is, how much the hope of eternal life avails, unto which he calls. And that you may know what the fulfilment of that hope is. Which he thus says: *And what are the riches.* Here he discloses what he understood by the name of hope: for he takes hope as the thing hoped for.

*What is the exceeding greatness.* The highest doctors shall have a certain increase of glory, beyond that which all shall have in common. For all shall have the same penny. *But star differeth from star in brightness ((I Cor. XV))*. *And there shall be diverse mansions in the house of the Father ((Joan. XIV))*.

*Raising him up,* etc. Now the example of the glory of the saints consists in the resurrection of the Saviour, that in it the faithful may know what has been promised to them. *At his right hand.* The right hand is the eternal beatitude which is given to the saints: the left is the misery which is given to the wicked. For by no form of body is God bounded and enclosed.

*Above every,* etc. This he says on account of the incarnation of the Son of God, that even having been made man he may be said to be above all the heavens, and above every creature, having his name by nature, not by adoption.

*Under his feet,* etc. By the feet full subjection is noted, and all things are deservedly subject to him, because they were made through him; or, the feet signify the humanity, because as the foot is the lower part of the body, so in Christ the lower nature is the humanity, which even the angels adore. *And him,* etc. After he has commemorated the dignity of Christ, he returns to us, showing that his dignity pertains to us; as if he should say: God so exalted Christ that this his exaltation pertains to us: because he himself is the head, and we the body, that we may partake of him. *The head.* According to the deity: because all were made by him, and also according to the humanity, by which the Church is joined to him, by nature and by grace. *For of his fullness we have all received ((Joan. X))*.

*His fullness.* Because he is filled up through them, yet being all things in all, here and in the time to come. Likewise. When those who have entered unto confession bend the knee to Christ, he is filled up, because those who withdraw seem to empty him. *All things in all.* Because the members confer nothing upon him, but he himself all things upon the members: because by his power they are what they are.

notes.text: And he said — On the day of his ascension. In the law, and the prophets, and the Psalms - The prophecies as well as types, relating to the Messiah, are contained either in the books of Moses (usually called the law) in the Psalms, or in the writings of the prophets; little being said directly concerning him in the historical books.

Then opened he their understanding, to understand the Scriptures — He had explained them before to the two as they went to Emmaus. But still they understood them not, till he took off the veil from their hearts, by the illumination of his Spirit.

Beginning at Jerusalem — This was appointed most graciously and wisely: graciously, as it encouraged the, greatest sinners to repent, when they saw that even the murderers of Christ were not excepted from mercy: and wisely, as hereby Christianity was more abundantly attested; the facts being published first on the very spot where they happened.
Behold I send the promise — Emphatically so called; the Holy Ghost.
He led them out as far as Bethany — Not the town, but the district: to the Mount of Olives, Acts i, 12, which stood within the boundaries of Bethany.

And while he was blessing them, he was parted from them — It was much more proper that our Lord should ascend into heaven, than that he should rise from the dead, in the sight of the apostles. For his resurrection was proved when they saw him alive after his passion: but they could not see him in heaven while they continued on earth. Please see Notes at Matt. i, 1

glossa.text: *Then he opened.* After the sight, after the touch, after the law recalled to mind, he opened their understanding, that they might understand what they see and read; then, after the truth of his own body had been commended, he commends the unity of the Church: *And that there should be preached in his name.*

*It behoved,* etc. It behoved that the ministers who were to preach penance and remission unto all nations should begin from Jerusalem. Not only because to them were entrusted the oracles of God, and because theirs is the adoption of sons, and the glory the testaments, and the law-giving; but for this reason also, that the Gentiles, entangled in various errors and crimes, might by this token above all of the divine loving-kindness be roused to the hope of pardon: that he grants pardon to those who crucified the Son of God.

*But stay you.* After he had perfectly instructed the disciples about the power of preaching, although he could of a sudden, if he willed, have strengthened them, he put it off, saying: *But stay you.* That he might give an example to those who follow, lest the imperfect presume to preach before the time. He sits in the city who binds himself within the cloisters of the mind, lest by speaking he wander abroad outside; so that when he has been perfectly clothed with the divine power, then he may go forth as it were out of himself, by instructing others.

*And he led them out.* Passing over all that was done through the forty days, he silently joins to the first day of the resurrection the last, on which he ascended into heaven. And beautifully, being about to bless the disciples, he leads them out to Bethany, which is called the house of obedience: because he who came down on account of the disobedience of the perverse, ascended on account of the obedience of the converted.

*In the temple.* That in the place of prayer, amid the devotions of praise, with hearts made ready in all things, they might await the promised coming of the Holy Spirit. So let us, after the solemnities of the passion and the resurrection have been celebrated in Jerusalem, that is, in the vision of peace, seek Bethany with the Lord for our leader, that with a quiet mind we may be steeped in the sacraments of his body and blood, and may take care to be a house of obedience.

*Praising and blessing.* Luke, who took upon himself to set forth Christ's priesthood more fully than the rest, and therefore began his Gospel from the ministry of the temple through the priesthood of Zachary, beautifully completed it in the devotion of the temple, when he concludes with the apostles there, ministers, namely, of the new priesthood to come, not in the blood of victims, but in the praise of God and in blessing.

Earth and heaven repeat the cry
Hail the day that sees him rise
Praise the Lord who reigns above

praise.title: O Praise Him (All This for a King)

echoes.text: “It will happen afterward, that I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh; and your sons and your daughters will prophesy. Your old men will dream dreams. Your young men will see visions. And also on the servants and on the handmaids in those days, I will pour out my Spirit. I will show wonders in the heavens and in the earth: blood, fire, and pillars of smoke. The sun will be turned into darkness, and the moon into blood, before the great and terrible day […]
echoes.note: The risen Jesus tells the apostles to wait for 'the promise of the Father' and the baptism 'in the Holy Spirit not many days from now.' Volume: no verbal quotation yet, but the conceptual content (an outpouring of the Spirit on God's people in the last days) maps directly onto Joel. Recurrence: decisive — Luke makes this same Joel text the explicit hermeneutical key at Pentecost (Acts 2:16-21), so the 'promise' here is programmatic foreshadowing. Thematic coherence: high; the whole opening frames the Spirit as eschatological gift. History of interpretation broadly reads the 'promise of the Father' as Joel's Spirit-pouring. Confidence high on Recurrence and Coherence even though the immediate Volume is thematic.

echoes.text: I will also give you a new heart, and I will put a new spirit within you; and I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you a heart of flesh. I will put my Spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes, and you shall keep my ordinances, and do them.
echoes.note: The Spirit 'put within' God's people to enable obedience is the other great prophetic promise standing behind 'the promise of the Father.' Volume is low (no shared wording in translation), but Thematic Coherence is strong: Ezekiel's interiorized Spirit is the renewal-of-Israel hope that the apostles' question in v.6 presupposes. Recurrence modest. Honestly faint relative to Joel, hence echo/medium.

echoes.text: Moses entered into the midst of the cloud, and went up on the mountain; and Moses was on the mountain forty days and forty nights.
echoes.note: Jesus appears and teaches 'over a period of forty days.' Volume: only the numeral, so verbal borrowing is minimal — this is a figural/typological link, not a citation. Thematic coherence: forty-day periods of divine revelation and preparation recur with Moses on Sinai (Exod 24:18; 34:28), Israel's wilderness, and Elijah (1 Kgs 19:8); Luke evokes a charged interval of instruction before a covenantal threshold. Recurrence: Luke uses forty-day patterning elsewhere (Jesus' temptation, Luke 4:2). Marked figural because the correspondence is structural, not lexical.

echoes.text: yes, he says, “It is too light a thing that you should be my servant to raise up the tribes of Jacob, and to restore the preserved of Israel: I will also give you for a light to the nations, that you may be my salvation to the end of the earth.”
echoes.note: 'You will be witnesses... to the uttermost parts of the earth' closely tracks the Servant's commission to be 'a light to the nations, that you may be my salvation to the end of the earth.' Volume: the phrase 'to the end(s) of the earth' is a distinctive LXX echo (heos eschatou tes ges). Recurrence: strong — Luke cites Isa 49:6 explicitly at Acts 13:47 and alludes again, making it a structural thesis statement for the book. Thematic coherence: very high; this verse programs Acts' whole geographic movement. A leading candidate in the history of interpretation for the key to Acts.

echoes.text: “You are my witnesses,” says Yahweh, “With my servant whom I have chosen; that you may know and believe me, and understand that I am he. Before me there was no God formed, neither will there be after me. I myself am Yahweh; and besides me there is no savior. I have declared, I have saved, and I have shown; and there was no strange god among you. Therefore you are my witnesses”, says Yahweh, “and I am God.
echoes.note: 'You will be witnesses to me' echoes the Lord's words to Israel, 'You are my witnesses... and my servant whom I have chosen.' Volume: the witness-language is distinctive and combined with election (the apostles 'whom he had chosen,' v.2). Recurrence: the witness motif saturates Acts. Thematic coherence: high; Israel's vocation to testify to the one God is transferred to the apostles. Overlaps with Isa 49:6 in the same Isaianic Servant matrix.

echoes.text: He changes the times and the seasons; he removes kings, and sets up kings; he gives wisdom to the wise, and knowledge to those who have understanding;
echoes.note: 'It isn't for you to know times or seasons (chronous e kairous) which the Father has set within his own authority' echoes Daniel's 'he changes times and seasons (kairous kai chronous)... he reveals deep and hidden things.' Volume: the paired words 'times and seasons' are a distinctive doublet shared with LXX Daniel. Thematic coherence: high; both texts locate the calendar of the kingdom in God's sovereign reserve. Recurrence: 'times and seasons' as a fixed pair recurs in Jewish apocalyptic. Solid mid-level link.

echoes.text: In that day I will raise up the tent of David who is fallen, and close up its breaches, and I will raise up its ruins, and I will build it as in the days of old; that they may possess the remnant of Edom, and all the nations who are called by my name,” says Yahweh who does this.
echoes.note: The apostles' question, 'are you now restoring the kingdom to Israel?', sits atop the prophetic hope of the rebuilt 'booth of David' that the remnant and the nations might seek the Lord. Volume: no shared wording here. Recurrence: notable — Luke quotes Amos 9:11-12 at the Jerusalem council (Acts 15:16-17) precisely to interpret how the restored Davidic kingdom includes the nations, which is exactly the tension between v.6 (Israel) and v.8 (the earth). Thematic coherence good; low confidence because the link is conceptual and back-referenced rather than verbal here.
echoes.lxxText: In that day I will raise up the tabernacle of David that is fallen, and will rebuild the ruins of it, and will set up the parts thereof that have been broken down, and will build it up as in the ancient days: that the remnant of men, and all the Gentiles upon whom my name is called, may earnestly seek me, saith the Lord who does all these things.

echoes.text: I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the ancient of days, and they brought him near before him.
echoes.note: 'A cloud received him out of their sight,' and the angels promise he 'will come back in the same way.' Volume: the cloud as the vehicle of the exalted Son of Man is the distinctive Danielic image (one 'coming with the clouds of heaven'). Luke reverses and reaffirms the trajectory — ascent now, return on clouds later. Recurrence: strong in Luke-Acts' Son-of-Man Christology (Luke 21:27; 22:69). Thematic coherence high; the cloud signals heavenly enthronement, the very kingship the disciples asked about in v.6.

echoes.text: As they still went on, and talked, behold, a chariot of fire and horses of fire separated them; and Elijah went up by a whirlwind into heaven.
echoes.note: Jesus 'was taken up' while the apostles 'looked steadfastly into the sky,' patterned on Elijah taken up to heaven as Elisha watched ('if you see me as I am taken from you...'). Volume: shared motif of a witnessed bodily assumption, the gaze of the successor(s), and the transfer of spirit/Spirit immediately afterward (Elisha's double portion ~ the apostles' Spirit-baptism). Recurrence: Luke deliberately uses Elijah-Elisha typology throughout (e.g., Luke 9:51, 9:61-62). Thematic coherence very high; the disciples' Spirit-empowerment in v.8 mirrors Elisha's inheritance. A staple of the history of interpretation.

echoes.text: His feet will stand in that day on the Mount of Olives, which is before Jerusalem on the east; and the Mount of Olives will be split in two, from east to west, making a very great valley. Half of the mountain will move toward the north, and half of it toward the south.
echoes.note: The ascension and promised return occur at/over the Mount of Olives (named in v.12), the very mountain on which 'the feet of the Lord' will stand on the eschatological day of his coming. Volume: low verbal overlap, but the geography is pointed and the angels' 'will come back in the same way' resonates with Zechariah's theophanic return to that mountain. Thematic coherence strong; recurrence modest. The setting makes this more than coincidental, hence echo/medium.

echoes.text: Enoch walked with God, and he was not found, for God took him.
echoes.note: Jesus' bodily removal to heaven faintly recalls Enoch, who 'walked with God, and he was not, for God took him' (LXX: 'God translated him'). Volume: low; only the shared motif of a righteous one taken without ordinary death. Recurrence: Enoch/assumption traditions were live in Second Temple Judaism. Coherence modest. Included as a faint, contested member of the 'assumption of the righteous' background alongside Elijah.

echoes.attribution: Catena, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wilson Pruitt / Wroot Press)

places.name: Jerusalem
places.id: The City of David and Old City, on the spurs above the Kidron Valley, c. 50 km from the Mediterranean. Pre-Israelite Jebus; named here as the seat of Adoni-Zedek, leader of the southern coalition.

places.name: Judea
places.id: The Roman administrative province (later procuratorial province) covering the southern hill country of Israel — Jerusalem, the Judean wilderness, and territory south to the Negev. The Greco-Roman successor to the Hasmonean and Herodian Iudaea. Pin sits in the central hill country.

places.name: Samaria
places.id: The central hill-country region between Galilee (north) and Judea (south), centered on the city of Sebaste / Samaria (Sebastiya) — the old capital of Omri (1 Kgs 16:24) refounded by Herod. Distinct from the city: pin sits in the regional centre.

places.name: Galilee
places.id: The northern region of Roman-period Palestine, bounded by the Jezreel valley (south), the Lebanese mountains (north), the Mediterranean (west), and the Jordan / Sea of Galilee (east). Subdivided into Lower Galilee (the Jesus traditions are mostly here) and Upper Galilee.

echoes.attribution: Catena, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wilson Pruitt / Wroot Press)

echoes.text: The Spirit of Yahweh will rest on him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of knowledge and of the fear of Yahweh.
echoes.note: 'A spirit of wisdom and revelation in the knowledge of him' draws on the Messianic 'Spirit of the LORD... the spirit of wisdom and understanding... the spirit of knowledge.' Volume is strong (spirit + wisdom + knowledge in sequence); thematic coherence (the endowing Spirit granting wisdom and knowledge of God) and the passage's Messianic availability make this a high-confidence allusion.

echoes.text: He changes the times and the seasons; he removes kings, and sets up kings; he gives wisdom to the wise, and knowledge to those who have understanding; he reveals the deep and secret things; he knows what is in the darkness, and the light dwells with him.
echoes.note: 'A spirit of wisdom and revelation' coheres with Daniel's God who 'gives wisdom to the wise... reveals deep and hidden things.' Recurrence of the Danielic wisdom/revelation pairing (cf. 1:9 mystery) supports a medium echo; the volume is moderate alongside the dominant Isaiah 11 source.

echoes.text: For this cause I prayed, and understanding was given me: I called upon God, and there came to me a spirit of wisdom.
echoes.note: 'I prayed, and understanding was given me; I called, and the spirit of wisdom came to me' (deuterocanonical) closely parallels praying for 'a spirit of wisdom' to know God. Thematic coherence is strong and the Wisdom tradition was available in Greek-speaking Judaism; medium because it is a parallel within a shared milieu rather than a citation.

echoes.text: You shall speak to all who are wise-hearted, whom I have filled with the spirit of wisdom, that they make Aaron’s garments to sanctify him, that he may minister to me in the priest’s office.
echoes.note: God filling artisans with a 'spirit of wisdom' to equip them is one OT background for Spirit-given wisdom granted to God's people. Availability is real but thematic coherence with revelatory knowledge of God is weaker than Isaiah 11; marked low and contested.

echoes.text: He filled them with the knowledge of wisdom, And showed them good and evil. He set his eye upon their hearts, To show them the majesty of his works.
echoes.note: Sirach's depiction of God enlightening humans with knowledge and 'setting his eye on their hearts' resonates faintly with 'the eyes of your hearts enlightened.' Availability within the wisdom corpus is genuine; volume and verbal overlap are low, so the echo is contested.

echoes.text: Yahweh’s precepts are right, rejoicing the heart. Yahweh’s commandment is pure, enlightening the eyes.
echoes.note: 'The commandment of the LORD is pure, enlightening the eyes' offers an OT idiom of divine illumination behind 'the eyes of your hearts enlightened.' Thematic coherence (God enlightening the perceiving faculty) is plausible; volume is faint, so low and contested.

echoes.text: Yahweh says to my Lord, “Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies your footstool for your feet.”
echoes.note: 'Made him to sit at his right hand in the heavenly places, far above all rule and authority' reproduces 'Sit at my right hand until I make your enemies your footstool.' Volume is very high (the most-cited OT verse in the NT); recurrence and thematic coherence (enthroned exaltation over all powers) make this a near-quotation undergirding the entire exaltation statement.

echoes.text: You make him ruler over the works of your hands. You have put all things under his feet:
echoes.note: 'He put all things in subjection under his feet' is a verbatim citation of 'you have put all things under his feet.' Volume is maximal (direct verbal match); recurrence (1 Cor 15:27; Heb 2:8) and thematic coherence (the dominion granted to the exalted man over creation) make this an explicit quotation.

echoes.text: Yahweh says to my Lord, “Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies your footstool for your feet.”
echoes.note: 'He put all things in subjection under his feet' also fulfills Psalm 110:1's 'until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet,' which Ephesians conflates with Psalm 8:6. The footstool/subjection imagery shows the two enthronement psalms read together; volume and thematic coherence (subjugation of enemies under the exalted Lord) are high.

echoes.text: so that the priests could not stand to minister by reason of the cloud; for Yahweh’s glory filled Yahweh’s house.
echoes.note: 'The fullness of him who fills all in all' evokes the glory of the LORD filling the temple so that 'the priests could not stand to minister.' Thematic coherence (divine presence filling God's house, now the church as body/temple) is strong; medium because the link is conceptual and joins other temple-glory texts.

echoes.text: Can any hide himself in secret places so that I shall not see him? says Yahweh. Don’t I fill heaven and earth? says Yahweh.
echoes.note: 'Do I not fill heaven and earth? says the LORD' supplies the divine self-description behind 'him who fills all in all.' Thematic coherence with God's omnipresent fullness is strong; the volume is moderate (a shared plerosis motif), so medium confidence.

echoes.text: In the year that king Uzziah died, I saw the Lord sitting on a throne, high and lifted up; and his train filled the temple. Above him stood the seraphim. Each one had six wings. With two he covered his face. With two he covered his feet. With two he flew. One called to another, and said, “Holy, holy, holy, is Yahweh of Armies! The whole earth is full of his glory!”
echoes.note: 'The whole earth is full of his glory,' with the temple filled by the LORD's train, reinforces the fullness/glory imagery of 1:23. Availability and thematic coherence (glory filling the sanctuary) support a faint echo; volume is low alongside 1 Kings 8 and Jeremiah 23, so contested.

echoes.text: Yahweh, our Lord, how majestic is your name in all the earth, who has set your glory above the heavens!
echoes.note: 'Head over all things' resonates with Psalm 8's exaltation of God's name 'above the heavens' and the dominion theme framing the quoted v.6. Thematic coherence (universal supremacy) is plausible; the volume is low and the link secondary to 8:6, so contested.

echoes.attribution: Catena, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wilson Pruitt / Wroot Press)

echoes.text: yes, he says, “It is too light a thing that you should be my servant to raise up the tribes of Jacob, and to restore the preserved of Israel: I will also give you for a light to the nations, that you may be my salvation to the end of the earth.”
echoes.note: The Servant given 'as a light to the nations, that my salvation may reach to the end of the earth' is the programmatic text behind 'repentance and remission of sins... to all the nations.' Luke quotes Isa 49:6 explicitly at Acts 13:47 and alludes to it at Acts 1:8, making it the key prophetic warrant for the worldwide mission launched here. Volume and recurrence are high.

echoes.text: “It will happen afterward, that I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh; and your sons and your daughters will prophesy. Your old men will dream dreams. Your young men will see visions.
echoes.note: 'I send out the promise of my Father on you... until you are clothed with power from on high' anticipates Joel's outpouring of the Spirit on all flesh, which Luke fulfills explicitly at Pentecost (Acts 2:17, quoting Joel). The Spirit as the Father's promise is the bridge from Luke 24 to Acts. Volume and recurrence are high.

echoes.text: All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to Yahweh. All the relatives of the nations shall worship before you.
echoes.note: That repentance and forgiveness be proclaimed 'to all the nations' fulfills the Psalter's vision that 'all the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the LORD,' part of the Writings (psalmoi) Jesus names as bearing witness to him. Luke roots the universal mission in the Psalms he has just cited. Coherence with the tripartite-canon statement supports it.

echoes.text: Many peoples shall go and say, “Come, let’s go up to the mountain of Yahweh, to the house of the God of Jacob; and he will teach us of his ways, and we will walk in his paths.” For out of Zion the law shall go out, and Yahweh’s word from Jerusalem.
echoes.note: 'Beginning at Jerusalem' enacts the eschatological pattern whereby 'out of Zion shall go forth the law, and the word of the LORD from Jerusalem,' the nations streaming to and the word streaming from Zion. Luke reverses the centripetal pilgrimage into a centrifugal mission from Jerusalem. Coherence is strong.

echoes.text: Many nations will go and say, “Come, and let us go up to the mountain of Yahweh, and to the house of the God of Jacob; and he will teach us of his ways, and we will walk in his paths.” For the law will go out of Zion, and Yahweh’s word from Jerusalem;
echoes.note: Micah's parallel oracle that 'the word of the LORD' goes forth 'from Jerusalem' to instruct the nations reinforces the Jerusalem-origin of the universal proclamation. The doubled prophetic witness (with Isa 2:3) strengthens the case that Luke draws on the Zion-mission tradition. Recurrence supports medium.

echoes.text: How beautiful on the mountains are the feet of him who brings good news, who publishes peace, who brings good news of good, who publishes salvation, who says to Zion, “Your God reigns!”
echoes.note: The herald who proclaims good news of salvation from Zion underlies Luke's commissioning of witnesses to preach forgiveness beginning at Jerusalem. Luke's vocabulary of proclaiming (kēryssō) good news echoes the Isaianic herald, a text central to his mission theology. Coherence good.

echoes.text: It will happen that whoever will call on Yahweh’s name shall be saved; for in Mount Zion and in Jerusalem there will be those who escape, as Yahweh has said, and among the remnant, those whom Yahweh calls.
echoes.note: 'Everyone who calls on the name of the LORD shall be saved... in Jerusalem there shall be those who escape' underwrites repentance/forgiveness proclaimed 'in his name' beginning from Jerusalem. Luke cites Joel 2 at Pentecost (Acts 2:21), making it a strong intertext for the commission. Recurrence in Luke-Acts supports it.

echoes.text: Until the Spirit is poured on us from on high, and the wilderness becomes a fruitful field, and the fruitful field is considered a forest.
echoes.note: 'Until the Spirit is poured upon us from on high' supplies the very phrase 'power from on high' (ex hypsous) for the promised Spirit-endowment. Luke's 'clothed with power from on high' draws on this Isaianic image of the Spirit poured out to renew. Verbal contact ('from on high') gives medium-strong confidence.

echoes.text: For I will pour water on him who is thirsty, and streams on the dry ground. I will pour my Spirit on your seed, and my blessing on your offspring:
echoes.note: 'I will pour my Spirit upon your descendants' reinforces the promised-Spirit theme of being clothed with power, an OT pattern of the Spirit poured out as gift and blessing. Together with Joel and Isa 32 it forms the cluster behind the Father's promise. Recurrence within the cluster supports it.

echoes.text: When Moses had made an end of writing the words of this law in a book, until they were finished, Moses commanded the Levites, who bore the ark of the covenant of Yahweh, saying, “Take this book of the law, and put it by the side of the ark of the covenant of Yahweh your God, that it may be there for a witness against you.
echoes.note: 'All things written in the law of Moses, the prophets, and the psalms... must be fulfilled' names the threefold Hebrew canon (Torah, Prophets, Writings), and the Law of Moses as a written witness placed beside the ark to testify is the Torah pole of that witness. Luke frames the whole of Scripture, beginning with Moses' written law, as testifying to Christ. Coherence with the canon formula supports it.

echoes.text: But the Spirit of Yahweh came on Gideon; and he blew a trumpet; and Abiezer was gathered together after him.
echoes.note: 'Clothed with power' (enedysasthe) recalls the idiom that the Spirit of the LORD 'clothed itself with' Gideon, the standard OT metaphor for divine empowerment of a chosen agent. Luke's clothing-with-power language may draw on this Spirit-clothing idiom. Faint verbal idiom, hence low and contested.

echoes.text: [source text not in the World English Bible]
echoes.note: The prologue to Sirach repeatedly names 'the Law and the Prophets and the others/the rest of the books,' the earliest explicit witness to the tripartite division of Hebrew Scripture that Luke 24:44 presupposes ('law of Moses, the prophets, and the psalms'). It supplies the Second-Temple canonical framework, not a content-quotation. Availability and coherence support medium.

echoes.text: Then he went down, and lifted up his hands Over the whole congregation of the children of Israel, To give blessing to the Lord with his lips, And to glory in his name. And he bowed himself down in worship the second time, To declare the blessing from the Most High. And now bless you the God of all, Which everywhere does great things, Which exalts our days from the womb, And deals with us according to his mercy.
echoes.note: Jesus 'lifted up his hands and blessed them' as he departs reproduces the climactic scene of Simon the high priest who 'lifted up his hands over the whole congregation... to pronounce the blessing of the LORD,' after which the people worship. Luke casts the ascending Jesus as the great high priest performing the Aaronic benediction. Volume, coherence, and the worship response all align strongly.

echoes.text: Aaron lifted up his hands toward the people, and blessed them; and he came down from offering the sin offering, and the burnt offering, and the peace offerings.
echoes.note: 'Aaron lifted up his hands toward the people and blessed them, and came down' is the priestly prototype for Jesus' parting gesture of lifted hands and blessing. The lifting-hands-to-bless is the defining act of the Aaronic priesthood, which Luke transfers to the ascending Christ. Verbal and gestural correspondence is high.

echoes.text: As they still went on, and talked, behold, a chariot of fire and horses of fire separated them; and Elijah went up by a whirlwind into heaven.
echoes.note: Jesus 'was carried up into heaven' while his disciples watch, closely paralleling Elijah taken up into heaven before Elisha, whose witnessing disciple then receives a double portion of his spirit. Luke's ascension-then-Spirit sequence is modeled on the Elijah-Elisha succession, and Luke uses Elijah typology throughout. Volume and coherence are high.

echoes.text: “Speak to Aaron and to his sons, saying, ‘This is how you shall bless the children of Israel.’ You shall tell them, ‘Yahweh bless you, and keep you. Yahweh make his face to shine on you, and be gracious to you. Yahweh lift up his face toward you, and give you peace.’ “So they shall put my name on the children of Israel; and I will bless them.”
echoes.note: The Aaronic blessing ('The LORD bless you and keep you...') is the content of the priestly benediction Jesus enacts with lifted hands. Luke evokes the priest putting the divine name on the people as the risen Christ blesses them at his departure. Coherence with the Lev/Sirach cluster supports it.

echoes.text: When they had gone over, Elijah said to Elisha, “Ask what I shall do for you, before I am taken from you.” Elisha said, “Please let a double portion of your spirit be on me.” He said, “You have asked a hard thing. If you see me when I am taken from you, it shall be so for you; but if not, it shall not be so.”
echoes.note: Elisha's request to inherit Elijah's spirit, granted 'if you see me taken,' parallels the disciples who witness Jesus' ascent and then await the promised Spirit. Luke ties the seeing of the departure to the bestowal of the Spirit, mirroring the Elijah-Elisha transfer. Recurrence with the prior verse supports medium.

echoes.text: God has gone up with a shout, Yahweh with the sound of a trumpet.
echoes.note: 'God has gone up with a shout' supplies the enthronement-ascent motif of God ascending to his throne amid praise, fitting the disciples who 'worshiped him and returned... with great joy, praising God.' Luke's ascension-to-worship sequence draws on the Zion enthronement psalms. Coherence with the joyful praise response supports it.

echoes.text: I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the ancient of days, and they brought him near before him. There was given him dominion, and glory, and a kingdom, that all the peoples, nations, and languages should serve him: his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom that which shall not be destroyed.
echoes.note: The ascent into heaven and the disciples' worship enact the giving of dominion and the service/worship of all peoples to the one like a son of man who comes with the clouds before the Ancient of Days. Luke's exalted Christ receiving worship realizes the Danielic enthronement. Coherence with the Son of Man framing of the chapter supports it.

echoes.text: Lift up your heads, you gates! Be lifted up, you everlasting doors, and the King of glory will come in. Who is the King of glory? Yahweh strong and mighty, Yahweh mighty in battle. Lift up your heads, you gates; yes, lift them up, you everlasting doors, and the King of glory will come in. Who is this King of glory? Yahweh of Armies is the King of glory! Selah.
echoes.note: The 'gates lift up your heads' entry of the King of glory was read in early tradition as the ascent of the exalted Lord into the heavenly sanctuary, paralleling Jesus carried up into heaven. Faint and traditional rather than verbal in Luke, so low and contested.

echoes.text: Enoch walked with God, and he was not found, for God took him.
echoes.note: Enoch who 'walked with God, and was not, for God took him' is an OT type of the righteous one assumed into heaven, contributing to the assumption pattern Luke narrates. As one of the canonical assumption figures (with Elijah) it faintly informs the ascension. Low, contested.

echoes.text: Moses and Aaron went into the Tent of Meeting, and came out, and blessed the people: and Yahweh’s glory appeared to all the people. Fire came out from before Yahweh, and consumed the burnt offering and the fat upon the altar. When all the people saw it, they shouted, and fell on their faces.
echoes.note: After Aaron's blessing the glory of the LORD appears and the people fall down/worship; Luke's sequence of priestly blessing followed by worship in the temple mirrors this Levitical pattern of blessing-then-glory-then-worship. Structural echo reinforcing the priestly reading, so low and supportive.

harmony.title: The Ascension
harmony.note: Luke alone tells it twice — at the end of his gospel and again at the opening of Acts.

registers.label: Spare
lines: Clap your hands, all you peoples.
God has gone up with a shout!
While he blessed them, he was lifted up.
And a cloud took him from their sight.
Why do you stand looking into heaven?
He will come in the same way.
Sing praises to our God and King. Come, let us worship.
Jesus is Lord of all!

registers.label: Immersive
lines: Lift your eyes with the disciples on the hill, watching his hands rise over you in blessing one last time.
God has gone up with a shout!
A cloud receives him, and the sky seems suddenly empty, and two strangers ask why you keep staring up.
God has gone up with a shout!
But he is not gone; he is enthroned, head over all things, filling everything in every way.
God has gone up with a shout!
So sound the trumpet, clap your hands, and sing: the one who walked our roads now reigns.
God has gone up with a shout! Jesus is Lord!

registers.label: Hybrid
lines: He lifted his hands and blessed them.
God has gone up with a shout!
A cloud took him; the sky stood open.
God has gone up with a shout!
He reigns now, head over all things.
God has gone up with a shout!
Come, let us worship the ascended Lord.
Jesus is Lord of all!
